title: White Nights
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
summary: Em São Petersburgo, durante as noites brancas do verão, um jovem solitário que vive mais nos sonhos do que na vida real encontra uma moça chorando à beira de um canal. Durante algumas noites os dois conversam, contam suas histórias e se tornam amigos. Uma história delicada sobre solidão, esperança e o amor.

chapters.title: A Lonely Dreamer
paragraphs: It was a wonderful night, the kind of night that only happens when we are young. The sky was full of stars and so bright that it was almost like day. These were the white nights of summer in St Petersburg, when the sun almost never goes down.

I was twenty-six years old, and I had lived in St Petersburg for eight years. But I didn't have a single friend. I lived alone in a small room with an old servant, Matryona. I was a lonely man and a dreamer. Every day I went to work, and every evening I walked through the streets of the city. I looked at the people and the buildings, and I imagined stories about them.

I knew many people by sight. There was an old man that I saw every day near the river. When he was not there, I worried about him. I even knew the houses. One house was my friend because it always looked happy. Another house was painted yellow, and I felt sad for it, because it was so ugly now.

That summer everybody left the city. They went to their country houses with their families, their furniture and their dogs. Every day I saw carts full of tables and chairs going out of town. After three days I felt completely alone. It was as if the whole city had forgotten me.
So one evening I walked out of the city too. I walked for hours among the fields and the little country houses. I felt free and happy, and I came back late at night, when the streets were empty.

As I was walking along the canal, I saw a young woman. She was leaning on the railing and looking down at the dark water. She wore a pretty yellow hat and a black coat. I walked past her quietly. Then I heard a soft sound. She was crying.
I stopped. My heart was beating fast. I wanted to say something kind, but I was very shy. I never talked to women. While I was still thinking, she turned and walked quickly away along the canal.

chapters.title: The First Night
paragraphs: I followed her, but on the other side of the street. Suddenly a man in a good coat came out of a side street. He was a little drunk, and he started to follow her. She walked faster and faster, but he was getting close.
I didn't think. I ran across the street with my big stick in my hand. The man saw me, and he went away without a word.
“Give me your arm,” I said to her. “He won't come back now.”
She took my arm. Her hand was shaking. “Thank you,” she said quietly.
“I am so happy that I could help you,” I said. “Please forgive me. I don't know how to talk to women. I have never talked to a woman before.”
She laughed a little. “Really? Never?”
“Never. I am always alone. I only dream about it. I dream that one day I will meet a woman, and I will tell her everything in my heart. And now I am talking to you, and I don't know what to say.”
“Well, I like you,” she said. “You are honest. But you must promise me something. You must not fall in love with me. We can only be friends. Do you promise?”
“I promise,” I said.
We walked slowly along the canal. The water was dark and quiet, and the sky was pale and silver.
“Why were you crying?” I asked.
“I can't tell you now,” she said. “Maybe tomorrow. Tell me, why are you so happy? Your face is shining.”
“Because I am talking to you,” I said. “Tonight I am alive. Tomorrow I can be sad again, but tonight I am happy.”
We walked to her street. At the door of her house she said, “I will be at the canal again tomorrow night at ten o'clock. You can come too, because I need a friend. But remember your promise.”
“I will come,” I said. “Tomorrow!”
I walked home through the bright night. For the first time in eight years I was not alone. I was so happy that I could not sleep.

chapters.title: The Story of a Dreamer
paragraphs: The next night I arrived at the canal at nine o'clock, one hour early. She came at ten.
“Now,” she said, sitting on a bench, “tell me your story. Who are you?”
“I have no story,” I said. “I am a dreamer. Do you know what a dreamer is?”
“No. Tell me.”

“A dreamer lives alone, in a little corner of the city, like a snail in its shell. In the day he works. But in the evening he comes home and lights his pipe, and then his real life begins. In his dreams he is a great poet or a hero. He travels to Italy. He falls in love with a beautiful woman. He has wonderful friends. His dreams are so real that he cries and laughs with them.
“But then the morning comes. He looks around his dirty little room, and he sees that his life is empty. Years go by, and he has nothing. No friends, no love, nothing real. Only dreams.”

“And sometimes,” I said, “the dreamer goes back to the places where he was happy in his dreams. He walks along the same streets and remembers. He is like an old man who looks at old letters. He thinks, 'Where are my years? What have I done with my life?' And he feels cold, because his best years have gone, and he has lived only in his head.”
I stopped. My face was red. “I'm sorry,” I said. “I talk like a book.”
She took my hand. “No,” she said softly. “I understand you. And I am happy that you told me. Now you are not alone. You have a friend. My name is Nastenka.”
“Nastenka!” I repeated. It was the most beautiful name in the world.
We sat on the bench and talked for a long time. She asked me many questions about my dreams, and she laughed at some of my answers. But it was a kind laugh. I felt that I had known her for years.
“You must not dream so much,” she said seriously. “You must live. Promise me that you will try.”
“With you, I don't need to dream,” I said. “With you, life is better than a dream.”
“And tomorrow,” she said, “I will tell you my story. You will see that I need your help.”

chapters.title: Nastenka's Story
paragraphs: “My parents died when I was very young,” said Nastenka. “I live with my grandmother. She is old and she is blind. She is afraid that I will do something silly, so she has pinned my dress to her dress. All day I sit next to her and read to her or knit.”
“Pinned?” I asked. I almost laughed.
“Yes, with a big pin. When she sleeps, sometimes I unpin it and run away for a few minutes. But not often.

“Once I wanted to play a joke on her. I asked our servant Fyokla to sit in my place, with the pin in her dress. Fyokla is deaf, so she can't hear anything. My grandmother started to ask questions, and of course Fyokla didn't answer. My grandmother was very angry when she discovered it. After that I never did it again.”

“Our house has a small room upstairs, and we rent it. A year ago a young man came to live there. He was quiet and kind. One day he gave my grandmother some books for me. I read them, and I loved them. Then he started to take us to the theater. In the dark theater, I fell in love with him.

“But one day he told my grandmother that he was going away to Moscow. He had to go for a year, for his work. He had no money. I cried all night. The night before he left, I took my things and went up to his room. I told him that I loved him, and I wanted to go with him.
“He held my hands and said, 'Nastenka, I love you too. But I am poor. I can't marry you now. Wait for me for one year. When I come back, if you still love me, we will marry.'
““And that was the night before he left. He promised me. He kissed my hand, and I gave him my word. I said I would wait for him.

“He left. And now the year has passed. He came back to St Petersburg three days ago. I know because I heard it from a friend. But he hasn't come to see me. He hasn't written a letter. Nothing. That's why I was crying by the canal.”
I listened in silence. My heart felt heavy. But I said, “Don't cry, Nastenka. Maybe he is busy. Write him a letter. I will take it to him.”
She smiled through her tears. She took a letter from her pocket. “I wrote it already,” she said.

chapters.title: The Third Night
paragraphs: I took the letter to the address of the young man. Then I went to the canal for our third meeting.
The weather was bad. It was raining, and the night was not so bright. Nastenka was waiting for me. Her eyes were shining.
“He will come tonight,” she said. “I'm sure. He has my letter now. He will come here to find me.”
“What did you say in your letter?” I asked.
“I wrote that he must come here tonight. He knows where the canal is. He will come.”

We waited and waited. She talked and laughed nervously. Every time somebody walked past, she jumped and looked at his face. But it was never him. She held my hand and said, “You are so good. You are like a brother to me. I wish he were like you!”
Every word hurt me, because I loved her. I had broken my promise. I fell in love with her on the very first night. But I said nothing.
The hours passed. Ten o'clock, eleven o'clock. He didn't come. At last Nastenka stood up. She looked tired and very sad.
“He isn't coming,” she said. “Maybe he never loved me.”
“Maybe he didn't get the letter in time,” I said. “Maybe he will come tomorrow.”
“Yes, tomorrow,” she said. “Come again tomorrow, please. I don't want to be alone.”
At her door she turned to me. “Thank you,” she said. “You are a true friend. I don't know what I would do without you.” Then she went inside.
I walked home in the rain. I thought only about her. I wanted her to be happy, but in my secret heart I hoped that the young man would never come.

chapters.title: The Fourth Night
paragraphs: On the fourth night Nastenka was waiting for me again. But he still didn't come, and she began to cry.
“How can he be so cruel?” she said. “He doesn't even write me one line!”

I couldn't keep my secret any more. “Nastenka,” I said, “forgive me. I have broken my promise. I love you. I loved you from the first night. I know you love him, and I know I have no chance. But I had to tell you.”

She was quiet for a long time. Then she took my hand. “I know,” she said softly. “I knew it. You are so good to me. He has forgotten me. Maybe... maybe in time I can love you too. I don't know. Let's not think about him any more.”
I couldn't believe it. We walked along the canal, and we were both happy. “Will you really stay with me?” I asked. My voice was shaking.
“Yes,” she said. “You love me, and he doesn't. I can see that now. You are the one who came to the canal every night. He didn't come once.”

We made plans. I would move into the room upstairs at her grandmother's house. We would be together, every day. We laughed like children. She talked about the books we would read together, and I talked about the places we would visit. For a few minutes we forgot everything. The night was beautiful, and the whole city was ours.
Then a young man walked past us. He stopped and looked back.
Nastenka's hand began to shake. “It's him!” she whispered.

She left me and ran to him. She threw her arms around his neck. Then, suddenly, she ran back to me and kissed me quickly. Without a word she went back to him, took his arm, and walked away with him down the street.
I stood alone by the canal and watched them go.

chapters.title: Morning
paragraphs: The next morning was dark and grey. Rain was falling on the window. My room looked old and dirty, and my head hurt.
Matryona brought me a letter. It was from Nastenka.

“Forgive me, please forgive me,” she wrote. “I was wrong to give you hope. I love him. I always loved him. But I love you too, like a brother, like a dear friend. I will never forget you. We are going to get married next week. Please come and visit us. Don't be angry with me. You will always be in my heart. Your Nastenka.”

I read the letter again and again. Tears came into my eyes. In the letter she also wrote: “I was confused. Last night I thought I could love you. But when I saw him, I knew that my heart was always his. Was it a dream? Please, don't hate me.”
“Hate you?” I said aloud to the empty room. “How could I hate you, Nastenka?”

Matryona was cleaning the room. She looked old to me that morning, much older than before. The walls looked dark. I saw my whole life in front of me, fifteen years from now, in the same little room, with the same Matryona, alone and old.
But I was not angry with Nastenka. How could I be angry? I didn't want her to have any pain because of me. I wished her a happy life, a life full of light and love.
“Be happy, Nastenka,” I thought. “Thank you for that one minute of happiness. You gave me a whole minute of joy. Isn't that enough for a whole lifetime?”
